stories.headline: Update: U.S. Completes Seventh Consecutive Night of Strikes Against Iran as Tehran Hits Allies, Attacks Syrian Base
stories.summary:
U.S. Central Command announced Friday night that it completed its seventh consecutive night of strikes against Iran, with operations beginning at 3 p.m. EDT and concluding at 9:30 p.m. ET. The military has widened its campaign in recent days to include bridges, energy sites, and infrastructure at a key Iranian port, with officials describing the goal as degrading Tehran's armed forces. The conflict shows no signs of abating, with shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz at its lowest level in more than a month and oil prices moving higher.

Iran struck back on Friday with new attacks on U.S. allies in the Middle East, including what was described as a first direct attack on a Syrian military base. Iranian officials warned that continued U.S. bombing could escalate into full-scale war. The Trump administration separately notified Israel it is sending dozens more refueling aircraft to the region, with the White House considering a significantly broader offensive against Iran.

The economic fallout is widening. An industry analyst said 'nobody is willing to move' through the Strait of Hormuz as the conflict disrupts global energy supply chains. The U.S. also backed a new Iraq-Syria oil pipeline deal with Chevron to create an alternative crude export route reducing reliance on the strait. Ceasefire talks that briefly paused the conflict have collapsed, with no resumption in sight.

The war has now entered what analysts describe as a dangerous new phase, with Washington expanding strikes beyond conventional military targets to infrastructure. The conflict is also reshaping British politics, with incoming Prime Minister Andy Burnham facing an immediate decision on how much to support Washington's campaign when he takes office next week.

stories.headline: Trump Urges Darline Graham to Run for Full Senate Term as President Backs Late Senator's Sister
stories.summary:
President Trump said Friday he met with newly appointed Sen. Darline Graham Nordone (R-S.C.) in the Oval Office and asked her to seek a full six-year Senate term in November's special election, posting on Truth Social that he asked her 'for the Good of our Nation' to run. Graham Nordone was sworn in earlier this week to fill the seat vacated by her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly on July 11 at his Washington home. She has no prior elected office experience; Lindsey Graham became her legal guardian when she was 13 after their parents died in quick succession.

Trump's endorsement effectively vaults Graham Nordone to the front of what had been shaping up as a crowded Republican primary field, though she had not yet publicly confirmed her candidacy as of Friday. The winner of the November special election will serve until January 2033. Graham's memorial services are scheduled for July 28 in Washington and July 29 in South Carolina.

The development is one of several reshaping the Senate landscape ahead of November's midterms. At least five and potentially as many as 13 current House members are expected to become senators next year through competitive races, retirements, and primary challenges, which could alter the chamber's culture and create friction with Senate leadership accustomed to slower deliberation.

stories.headline: ICE Processing Center Employee Arrested on Attempted Murder Charge After Shooting Protester in Colorado
stories.summary:
A GEO Group employee at the Aurora ICE Processing Center in Colorado was arrested Friday on charges of attempted second-degree murder and assault after police say he shot and wounded a woman during a protest outside the facility Thursday night. Brandon Booth, 42, was taken into custody in a vehicle less than two blocks from the scene; a gun was found inside the vehicle. Aurora Police Chief Todd Chamberlain called the shooting a 'tragedy on all fronts.'

According to police, Booth was waiting with fellow employees who could not access the facility due to the protest when two women approached, took photographs of employees' vehicles, and walked away. Booth then retrieved his personal firearm and fired a single shot, striking one of the women in the lower body. Her injuries were described as non-life-threatening. GEO Group placed Booth on unpaid administrative leave and said it would cooperate fully with law enforcement.

The shooting intensifies an already fraught national debate over immigration enforcement and the treatment of ICE detention facilities. Immigrants' rights advocates who gathered Friday at the Colorado Attorney General's office cited the incident as evidence of inadequate vetting and oversight of detention center staff. The incident adds to a series of recent confrontations involving ICE personnel that have drawn scrutiny from congressional Democrats and calls for a review of agency hiring practices.

stories.headline: EU Proposes Slowing Business Carbon Emission Cuts, Extending Free Permits to 2038 in Major Climate Policy Overhaul
stories.summary:
The European Commission unveiled proposals Friday that would ease and slow the pace of carbon emission reductions required of European businesses under the bloc's Emissions Trading System, the EU's primary tool for cutting greenhouse gases since 2005. Under the plan, industries could continue receiving free emission permits until 2038 rather than 2034, and the annual rate at which the cap on total permits is reduced would be lowered from the current 4.3% to 3.7% beginning in 2031, then to 1.7% from 2036. The proposals still require approval from EU member states and the European Parliament, a process expected to take roughly a year.

EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra framed the changes as a 'more business-friendly and savvy approach,' aligning the trading system with the EU's goal of 90% emissions reduction by 2040 compared to 1990 levels. The revisions come amid pressure from member states, particularly Italy and Poland, which have criticized the ETS as an effective tax inflating energy costs and undermining industrial competitiveness. Polish climate minister Paulina Hennig-Kloska welcomed the proposals but said Poland would push for further weakening.

Environmentalists and Green politicians sharply criticized the plan. German MEP Michael Bloss warned the reforms would result in 'gigantic climate pollution' and worsen quality of life for future generations. The overhaul marks a notable shift in EU climate governance, with the bloc's executive arm openly prioritizing business relief over accelerated decarbonization timelines for the first time since the ETS was established.

stories.headline: China's Moonshot AI Releases Kimi K3, Closing Gap With Top U.S. Models
stories.summary:
Beijing-based Moonshot AI unveiled Kimi K3 on Thursday, a massive open-source artificial intelligence model that developers say matches or rivals cutting-edge offerings from leading American firms such as Anthropic, at substantially lower cost. The release immediately drew comparisons to the DeepSeek disruption earlier in the AI race, jolting Silicon Valley and prompting fresh debate about whether the United States retains a commanding lead in frontier AI development.

Kimi K3 vaulted into the top tier of global AI benchmarks upon release and is freely available, a move that analysts say could undercut the pricing power of U.S. commercial AI providers. The development comes as Washington has imposed sweeping chip export controls intended to slow China's AI progress, raising questions about the effectiveness of those restrictions.

The release renews a central policy debate: whether America's AI advantage — built on massive private investment, top research talent, and access to the most advanced semiconductors — can be sustained as Chinese firms demonstrate the ability to achieve competitive results through alternative architectural approaches and efficiency gains. Proponents of the export controls argue they remain necessary to slow military AI applications; critics contend the controls have failed to prevent frontier-level civilian AI development in China.

The announcement is expected to intensify congressional and White House scrutiny of U.S. AI competitiveness strategy and may accelerate calls for increased federal investment in domestic AI research and infrastructure.

stories.headline: Federal Appeals Court Strikes Down New Jersey's AR-15 and High-Capacity Magazine Bans
stories.summary:
The Third U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Friday, by a 10-5 vote, that New Jersey's bans on assault-style firearms and high-capacity magazines violate the Second Amendment. The decision represents one of the most significant legal victories for gun rights advocates since the Supreme Court's 2022 Bruen ruling, which established a historical-tradition test for evaluating firearms regulations.

The ruling invalidates restrictions that New Jersey Democrats had defended as essential public safety measures backed by evidence linking high-capacity weapons to mass casualty events. Gun rights advocates hailed the decision as a proper application of constitutional precedent, arguing that commonly owned semi-automatic rifles and standard-capacity magazines are protected arms under the Second Amendment.

Opponents of the ruling, including gun control organizations and New Jersey state officials, condemned the decision and indicated they would pursue further legal challenges, potentially seeking Supreme Court review. They argue that assault weapon bans reflect a legitimate government interest in limiting the lethality of mass shootings and that courts are ignoring the public health consequences of unrestricted access to military-style weapons.

The ruling adds to a growing body of post-Bruen circuit court decisions striking down state-level gun restrictions, increasing pressure on the Supreme Court to provide clearer guidance on the permissible scope of such regulations. Similar bans in other states, including California and Maryland, remain under legal challenge.

stories.headline: Wisconsin Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez Drops Out of Governor's Race Over Financial Reporting Errors
stories.summary:
Wisconsin Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez announced Friday she is suspending her Democratic gubernatorial campaign after her campaign disclosed major inaccuracies in its financial reporting. Rodriguez had been considered a leading contender in the Democratic primary to succeed retiring Gov. Tony Evers in a state widely viewed as a critical battleground in national politics.

The withdrawal shakes up a primary in which Rodriguez represented the moderate, establishment wing of the Democratic Party. Party strategists expressed concern that her exit could strengthen the position of Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, in a purple state where Democrats have historically relied on centrist positioning to win statewide races.

The nature of the financial reporting errors was not fully specified, but Rodriguez indicated the irregularities would have created ongoing complications for the campaign. The disclosure follows increased scrutiny of campaign finance compliance at all levels of American politics.

Wisconsin's 2026 governor's race is considered a significant contest for both parties as Democrats seek to defend a foothold in the Midwest and Republicans aim to flip the statehouse. The primary outcome will be closely watched as a signal of which direction Wisconsin Democrats choose to move heading into the general election.

stories.headline: Andy Burnham Officially Declared UK Labour Leader, Set to Become Prime Minister Next Week
stories.summary:
Andy Burnham was formally declared leader of Britain's governing Labour Party on Friday, clearing the final procedural hurdle before he takes office as prime minister next week. The former Greater Manchester mayor was the sole contender in the leadership contest to replace Keir Starmer, who resigned last month after a party rebellion driven by plummeting poll numbers and a string of political missteps. Burnham secured nominations from 379 of the 403 Labour members of Parliament.

In his first speech as party leader, Burnham pledged to restore hope to communities "who have been waiting too long for politics to let them hope again" and promised to decentralize power from Westminster to local governments across England. He called for an end to Labour's internal factionalism, warning the party it "won't beat Britain's new right if we are consumed by infighting."

Burnham inherits a party trailing badly behind the anti-immigration Reform UK in opinion polls, following catastrophic results in May's local elections. He faces immediate challenges including a sluggish economy, a cost-of-living crisis, and overstretched public services — the same structural problems that ultimately felled Starmer. His pledges of a less divisive, more communicative leadership style echo Starmer's own promises upon taking office, raising questions among commentators about whether a change in personality can drive a change in political fortunes.

Burnham is largely unknown to voters outside Manchester, having spent recent years as a regional mayor rather than in national government. His arrival at 10 Downing Street next week will mark the second Labour prime minister in two years and the first major leadership transition in a governing party since the current political cycle began.

stories.headline: Magnitude 7.3 Earthquake Strikes Off Mexico's Southern Coast, Tsunami Warning Issued and Lifted
stories.summary:
A powerful magnitude 7.3 earthquake struck off the coast of southern Mexico near the fishing town of Puerto Madero in Chiapas state at 8:49 a.m. local time Friday, triggering a tsunami warning across parts of the Pacific Coast. The U.S. Tsunami Warning System initially warned of potentially hazardous waves along the coasts of Mexico and Guatemala; waves of approximately 0.3 meters above tide level were recorded at Puerto Madero and in Chiapas before the threat was declared passed several hours later.

Mexico's navy secretary Admiral Raymundo Morales said there was "no serious impact" from the quake, and governors of both Oaxaca and Chiapas reported no significant structural damage or fatalities. Residents in Guatemala and El Salvador reported buildings shaking and triggered evacuations, with Guatemala's President Bernardo Arévalo activating emergency management services in response to a secondary 5.6-magnitude tremor centered in Quetzaltenango. No deaths have been confirmed in any affected country.

A series of aftershocks ranging from magnitude 4.7 to 6.0 followed the initial quake. NOAA forecast waves of less than 0.3 meters along the coasts of eight additional Central and South American nations including El Salvador, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Nicaragua, Panama, Peru and Honduras. Authorities in affected areas advised populations to stay away from beaches while monitoring continued.

The quake struck at a shallow depth of 15.2 kilometers, which typically amplifies surface shaking. Mexico's Pacific coast sits along one of the world's most seismically active zones; the country has suffered multiple deadly earthquakes in recent decades, making today's limited damage a significant relief.

stories.headline: Tanker Hijacked in Gulf of Aden Off Yemen in Second Piracy Incident Since May
stories.summary:
Pirates seized a tanker in the Gulf of Aden off the coast of Yemen on Friday in what maritime officials are calling the second successful hijacking in the region since May and part of a broader resurgence of Somali piracy. The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) confirmed a vessel was boarded by unauthorized personnel traveling east and advised all nearby ships to transit with caution. Puntland security officials identified the vessel as the MT Astana, a Tanzanian-flagged tanker, seized by seven gunmen approximately 65 nautical miles off Yemen.

The attackers departed from a remote area near the Puntland port town of Garacad before moving into the Gulf of Aden, according to three separate Puntland security officials who spoke to the BBC. The MT Astana was en route to the port of Bosaso in Puntland when it was boarded. This incident follows the May seizure of the MT Eureka near Yemen's port of Qana, and two additional boardings in the Indian Ocean in April.

The Gulf of Aden has historically been less heavily patrolled than the Indian Ocean, which is monitored by the EU Naval Force's anti-piracy operation. Security officials say this protection gap may explain why pirates have shifted their operations to the Gulf. Until approximately three years ago, piracy in the region had largely been suppressed following sustained multinational naval operations that began over a decade ago.

The resurgence comes as the Gulf of Aden and surrounding waters are already under heightened tension due to ongoing Houthi attacks on commercial shipping — a separate but destabilizing factor for global maritime trade through one of the world's busiest sea lanes.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Fights Under Interim Defense Chief as Protests Erupt Over Fedorov Dismissal
stories.summary:
Ukraine entered Friday operating without a confirmed defense minister after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's surprise dismissal of Mykhailo Fedorov triggered public protests and exposed a deep generational rift within the country's military establishment. Zelenskyy designated Maj. Gen. Yevhen Khmara, acting head of the state security service and a decorated special operations officer, to serve in an acting capacity, and said he would formally nominate Khmara to parliament — though confirmation faces procedural hurdles, including a legal requirement that the defense minister be a civilian and a parliamentary recess that runs through mid-August.

Fedorov, 35, had served six months as defense minister and was widely credited with accelerating Ukraine's drone warfare capabilities and reducing military procurement corruption. Zelenskyy said the dismissal stemmed from an irreparable breakdown between Fedorov and Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi, the 60-year-old commander of Ukraine's armed forces, framing the conflict as one between old-guard military thinking and younger technological innovators. Thousands of demonstrators took to streets in multiple Ukrainian cities Thursday and Friday, with signs reading 'Don't ruin something that works.'

The shake-up comes at a sensitive moment: Ukraine has in recent months gained battlefield traction, and the leadership vacuum — however temporary — raises questions about continuity in procurement and drone strategy. Fedorov defended his record Friday, writing on social media that Ukraine had been 'transformed into a global tech leader and a defense powerhouse' during his tenure.

The reshuffle also included the appointment of a new prime minister, compounding the scale of the government overhaul. Analysts noted the timing is particularly fraught given ongoing uncertainty about U.S. support levels and the recent death of Senator Lindsey Graham, whom Ukraine had considered a key American advocate.

stories.headline: ICE Officer in Maine Shooting Had Documented History of Mental Health Issues, Family Says
stories.summary:
The Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who fatally shot a Colombian man in Maine this week is an Army veteran whose close relatives told the Associated Press he has struggled with serious mental health issues since early childhood and should never have been given a badge and gun. The AP obtained records corroborating family accounts of violent behavior, in what the outlet is describing as exclusive reporting on the officer's background. Lawmakers from both parties have called for answers following the incident.

The Maine shooting is one of several recent high-profile incidents involving ICE agents that have drawn national scrutiny, including a fatal shooting in Houston and footage of agents tackling a man at the Las Vegas airport. President Trump had directed ICE to resume traffic stops despite the two recent deadly shootings, a decision that Democrats have criticized as reckless and that immigration enforcement advocates have defended as necessary to carry out the administration's deportation mandate.

The AP report adds new pressure on the administration to address vetting and mental health screening standards within ICE, an agency that has significantly expanded its operations and personnel under Trump. Republican defenders of ICE argue isolated incidents should not be used to undermine the broader enforcement mission, while Democratic critics contend a pattern of incidents points to systemic failures in hiring and oversight.

The story is drawing coverage from six outlets and comes as Congress continues to press the administration on ICE conduct. A vigil was planned for the Houston victim, and Fedorov's family was expected to speak publicly about the Maine case.

stories.headline: Trump Media to Sell High-Speed 'Truth API' Feed of Posts to Wall Street Firms
stories.summary:
Trump Media & Technology Group, the company behind Truth Social, announced it will launch a paid commercial data service beginning August 1 that delivers posts from the platform's highest-ranking accounts to institutional financial clients in milliseconds. The service, called Truth API, is designed to give banks and trading firms faster access to posts that can move markets — most notably those from President Trump, who currently holds the largest follower count on the platform and whose posts frequently cause sudden swings in global equities and commodity prices, particularly on trade and tariff matters.

Acting CEO Kevin McGurn said the service would create a steady revenue stream for the currently loss-making company. Trump Media did not disclose pricing. The company also warned it would soon block firms that have been copying its data without permission, effectively compelling them to purchase the official feed. Because Trump's family remains the majority shareholder in Trump Media, the president stands to benefit financially from selling expedited access to his own public statements — a conflict-of-interest concern that ethics observers flagged immediately.

Legal experts told Reuters that while the arrangement may be ethically unusual, it does not appear to violate federal securities laws, as platforms are generally permitted to tier the distribution of their data. Investment analyst Mark Spiegel of Stanphyl Capital noted that Trump's posts represent only a fraction of market-moving information, but acknowledged firms could be 'at a disadvantage' if they declined to subscribe. The White House declined to comment on whether Trump's own posts would be included in the paid feed.

The announcement highlights the unusual overlap between the president's private financial interests and his public communications. Critics argue selling expedited access to presidential statements to select paying customers creates an uneven informational playing field and raises novel questions about market integrity that regulators have not previously confronted.

stories.headline: Update: Epstein Survivors Call Meeting with AG Nominee Blanche 'Demoralizing' as Confirmation Hangs in Balance
stories.summary:
Multiple survivors of Jeffrey Epstein's abuse said a meeting with attorney general nominee Todd Blanche on Thursday felt perfunctory and unsatisfying, describing it as a box-checking exercise rather than a substantive engagement. The meeting was convened after retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) announced he would withhold his vote on the Senate Judiciary Committee until Blanche met with survivors — a threat that held significant weight, as a single Republican "no" vote would have been enough to block Blanche's nomination from advancing to the full Senate.

Survivors told reporters the conversation moved quickly and left them without confidence that the Justice Department under Blanche would aggressively pursue accountability in the Epstein case. However, at least one participant — Jennifer Bos — said Blanche's remarks gave her reason to believe he understood the concerns of victims' families, suggesting the meeting produced mixed reactions among those who attended.

Blanche's confirmation to lead the Justice Department remains consequential given the scope of ongoing federal investigations and the politically charged nature of the Epstein files. Supporters argue Blanche, who previously served as Trump's personal defense attorney, brings legal experience to the role and has pledged cooperation with survivors. Critics, including Senate Democrats, have questioned whether he can act as an independent law enforcement officer given his prior representation of the president.

stories.headline: More Than 500 Rohingya Feared Dead After Two Boats Vanish at Sea
stories.summary:
Two boats carrying an estimated 530 Rohingya asylum seekers departed Myanmar's Rakhine State on June 29 and have not been heard from since, with humanitarian researchers now concluding it is very likely both vessels capsized with few or no survivors. The boats left Sin Tet Maw, an area controlled by the Arakan Army insurgent group, during the monsoon season when seas are particularly dangerous. A single body has been recovered by Bangladeshi authorities, and fishermen found several more floating in waters between the Irrawaddy delta and the coast of Mon State roughly nine days after the boats' departure.

The Arakan Project, a Rohingya advocacy organization, said its director Chris Lewa pieced together the timeline through intermediary contacts after direct communications with Rakhine were severed by Myanmar's military. The boats were overcrowded converted fishing trawlers with unreliable engines, heading south toward Thailand and ultimately Malaysia, where roughly 200,000 Rohingyas already reside. Families expected to hear from passengers within 10 days; nearly three weeks have passed in silence.

Rakhine State has been engulfed in conflict between Myanmar's military junta and the Arakan Army, which has driven government forces from most of the region. Rohingyas face forced conscription by the military and documented human rights abuses by the Arakan Army, while more than one million others remain in overcrowded camps in southern Bangladesh with diminishing humanitarian aid. The potential loss of 530 people would represent one of the deadliest Rohingya maritime disasters on record.

stories.headline: Philippines Condemns Chinese State Media Video Depicting Country as Monkey in South China Sea Dispute
stories.summary:
The Philippines has formally condemned an AI-generated video published by China Daily that depicted the Philippines as a frightened monkey wearing a Filipino shirt, being manhandled by figures representing the United States and Japan in a South China Sea context. The video, posted on July 10, shows the monkey-figure being thrown into the sea and blasted by a water cannon after attempting to present a South China Sea arbitration award — a direct reference to the 2016 Permanent Court of Arbitration ruling that found China's expansive maritime claims had no basis in international law. China has ignored that ruling.

Manila's foreign ministry called the imagery "dehumanising and racist" and demanded the video be removed, stating that disagreements over legal and political issues do not justify "disturbing imagery" in public discourse. Philippine Defence Secretary Gilbert Teodoro called the clip "contemptible propaganda" that exposed the "moral and intellectual bankruptcy of China's propaganda machine." As of the time of reporting, the video remained on China Daily's Facebook page.

The video's publication coincides with the tenth anniversary of the arbitration ruling, a milestone Beijing has used to restate its position that the tribunal lacked jurisdiction. Tensions between Manila and Beijing have escalated sharply in recent years, with confrontations at sea involving water cannons, physical altercations, and in June, China barring the Philippine defence secretary and his family from entering Chinese territory. The episode adds a new dimension of information warfare to the ongoing territorial dispute.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Expands Iran Strikes to Infrastructure as Ceasefire Collapses
stories.summary:
The United States escalated its military campaign against Iran overnight into Friday, striking bridges in Iran's southern Hormozgan province and hitting targets further north, including on Greater Tunb Island. The strikes mark a significant shift in American targeting strategy, with President Trump having threatened to attack civilian infrastructure to pressure Tehran into easing its chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian state television reported at least seven people killed in the bridge strikes, while U.S. Central Command said it also fired on a ship attempting to break the U.S. naval blockade reimposed Wednesday.

Iran retaliated with missile and drone fire targeting U.S.-allied nations including Bahrain, Kuwait, and Qatar — a key mediator in the conflict. Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf warned Tehran was prepared for full military confrontation if Washington did not honor the terms of the now-collapsed interim deal. Iranian officials say U.S. strikes since the latest round of violence began have killed more than 35 people and wounded over 300.

The interim ceasefire, agreed to last month, has fully unraveled, returning the region to a state of active war. The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed to commercial shipping, with U.S. forces redirecting or disabling vessels attempting to breach the blockade. The closure has sent global oil prices soaring, with ripple effects on the cost of fuel, food, and consumer goods worldwide.

In a primetime address to the American public, Trump insisted the war was progressing favorably, saying 'We are likewise winning big in Iran, and you will see the fruits of that labor very, very shortly.' Critics, including Senate Democrats who have moved to block defense legislation, argue the administration lacks a clear exit strategy and that rising energy prices pose a mounting political liability ahead of November's midterm elections.

stories.headline: At Least 20 Children Killed in Uganda School Bus Crash
stories.summary:
At least 20 students and one adult were killed Thursday evening when a bus carrying pupils on a study trip crashed in the Kapchorwa district of eastern Uganda. Preliminary investigations indicate the bus suffered a mechanical fault before the driver lost control on Chekwatit Hill, a stretch of road that has been the site of several prior serious accidents. The adult killed was identified as Tadeo Ssekade, the founder and director of King David Junior School in Ndejje, whose students were on board.

Decades of injury were also reported among students and staff. The bus was returning from a visit to Sipi Falls, a tourist destination, when it veered off the road, struck a large stone, and overturned. Ugandan authorities suspended all school educational trips pending a full investigation into the crash.

Education Minister John Chrysostom Muyingo called for immediate action on child transport safety following the disaster. Uganda records thousands of road deaths annually, with speeding, poorly maintained vehicles, and dangerous road conditions cited as leading causes. Officials noted the crash comes amid renewed concern over school transport safety after several serious bus accidents in the country in recent weeks.

stories.headline: Update: Canadian Wildfire Smoke Triggers Hazardous Air Quality Alerts Across U.S. Northeast and Midwest
stories.summary:
More than 858 wildfires burning across Canada, including 30 that ignited Thursday, have pushed a thick blanket of smoke across major U.S. cities, triggering hazardous air quality alerts from Chicago and Detroit to New York and across New England. Cities including Pittsburgh, Toledo, Grand Rapids, and Chicago registered dangerous readings on the U.S. Air Quality Index, prompting officials to cancel outdoor events, close beaches, and urge residents to remain indoors.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared the situation 'a very serious health situation,' noting that smoke was blanketing the state and making outdoor activity 'very unhealthy' in many areas. New York City activated air quality emergency protocols and opened hundreds of cooling centers while distributing KN95 masks. Iconic city landmarks including the Empire State Building and the Statue of Liberty were obscured by haze.

In Canada, at least one First Nations community in northern Ontario was evacuated after fire burned through the area, with a local chief describing her community as 'burnt to ashes.' Forecasters warned that northwesterly winds would continue driving smoke into northern U.S. states through the weekend, raising concerns it could affect conditions around New Jersey, where Sunday's World Cup final is scheduled to take place.

stories.headline: Japan Passes Historic Imperial Succession Reform, Female Emperors Still Barred
stories.summary:
Japan's parliament passed landmark legislation Friday allowing the imperial family to adopt distant male relatives over the age of 15 and permitting female members to retain their royal status after marrying outside the family. The bill, which cleared the upper house Friday after passing the lower house last week, represents the most significant overhaul of Japan's Imperial House Law since 1949 and comes amid mounting concern over the dwindling number of eligible successors to the Chrysanthemum Throne.

Despite the reforms, the bill does not permit women to ascend to the throne, leaving Princess Aiko — the only child of reigning Emperor Naruhito — ineligible to succeed her father. Currently, the line of succession runs through Emperor Naruhito's younger brother Fumihito, his 19-year-old son Prince Hisahito, and the Emperor's 90-year-old uncle, who is the last eligible candidate under existing rules. Without a male heir from Prince Hisahito, the succession line would otherwise end.

Opinion polls show broad public support for allowing a female emperor, with surveys by Mainichi Shimbun and Kyodo News finding between 70% and 83% of respondents in favor. Conservative political leaders, including Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, have argued male-only succession is essential to imperial legitimacy. The new law will allow male descendants of 11 imperial branches dissolved after World War Two to be adopted back into the family, expanding the pool of eligible future heirs.
